The session begins.

The sun is sliding down behind the Outer City and the shadows of the gatehouse stretch across the Trade Way. The queue shuffles forward a cart's length at a time: a family with their whole life on a handcart, a dwarf swearing at his mule, two sellswords comparing scars. Up ahead, under the arch, a Flaming Fist sergeant with a ledger and a tired voice asks everyone the same thing: name, business, how long you're staying.

From the side of the road comes a familiar sound — cards being shuffled. A lean young woman has turned a crate into a table and is dealing for anyone with copper to lose. "Short wait, quick game, friend! Lady Luck's smiling tonight!" Her eyes have already found James's coat and the weight of his purse.

At your feet the cat has gone very still. It is not looking at the cards on the crate. It is looking at the notice board beside the gate, where, between a wanted poster and a notice about curfew in the Upper City, someone has pinned a single playing card — face out, alone, without a word of explanation.

The sergeant looks up from his ledger. "Next." Two more travellers and it will be you.

James doesn't step out of the line. The dealer laughs, quick and bright, and her hands never stop moving.

"Then she's smiling at the wrong man, friend. I'm the one she's paying tonight." She fans the deck, closes it, and fans it again. "Offer stands while the line does."

James looks past her, past the dwarf's mule, to the notice board. It's maybe thirty feet away, close to forty, half in the long shadow of the arch. The cat hasn't moved. Its tail is wrapped tight around its paws.

The cart ahead rolls forward, and the last of the sun slips under the arch and strikes the board at a low angle. For a moment James sees the card clearly.

It isn't pasteboard. Pasteboard curls and goes soft at the corners in the damp off the river, and this card hasn't. It hangs flat and stiff and has a faint yellowish sheen, like old bone or ivory, thin enough that the light almost comes through at the edges. Someone painted it by hand. James has held thousands of cards, and no printer's block makes lines that fine.

The face shows a woman in a veil, and she has two faces under it. One looks straight out at the street, smiling. The other is turned away in profile, so all you see is a cheek and the line of a jaw, as if she's listening to someone behind her. She holds a coin up between finger and thumb, edge-on to the viewer, so you can't tell which side is up. There's no suit and no number on it, and no word or price on it anywhere. Whoever pinned it put a single iron tack through the top margin and kept it carefully clear of the painting.

James has played a good many decks between Tethyr and the Sword Coast, and he has never seen this card in any of them.

Then the light is gone. In the same moment the Coin of Tymora at his throat goes cold against his skin, the way a coin feels when it has just come out of someone else's hand. It lasts the space of a breath, and then it's just metal warmed by his own body again.

The cat still hasn't looked away from the card.

"Next." The sergeant turns a page in his ledger without looking up. One traveller is left between James and the arch: the dwarf, who is now arguing with his mule about whether it will walk under the stone.

The dwarf gets his mule under the arch with a slap on the rump and a word that makes the family behind him cover a child's ears. Then the sergeant is in front of James. He's a heavy man in a faded red tabard, with ink on two fingers and a ledger that has seen too many hands today.

"James Worgen," the sergeant repeats, and writes it down. His letters are square and slow. "Lodgings and work. As long as it holds." He writes that too, word for word, as if he's heard it a thousand times.

His eyes go to the cat for a moment, then to the purse at James's belt. The pen stops. Beside the entry, in the margin, he makes a small mark, a short slanted stroke, and then he's writing again as if he never paused.

At the question about the board he doesn't look round.

"Not Fist business." He blots the line. "Board-man takes a copper, anything goes up. Cards go up now and then. Lower City business. They're for somebody." Now he does look up, flat and tired. "Somebody's not usually the man asking."

Off to the side, Tamsin has stopped dealing. She doesn't pretend she wasn't listening.

"He's right, friend, it's not a lost-and-found." She taps the top of her deck with one finger. "But I know what it says on the back. One hand and I'll tell you. Win or lose, you still get your answer."

The sergeant ignores her, the way you ignore a fly that's been there all day. He turns the ledger a quarter-turn and holds out his ink-stained hand, palm up.

"Gate toll's a silver. Animal's another two." The cat hasn't moved its eyes from the notice board. "Three silver, and you're in."

Sergeant Vask's ink-stained hand closes around the gold piece. He doesn't bite it or even look at it. He drops it into a dented tin box at his elbow and counts the change out of the same tin, one silver at a time, onto James's palm.

"Seven." He's already looking past James's shoulder. "In. Next."

Behind him, Tamsin's cards go on whispering on the crate.

"A promise." She says it lightly, like a trick she's seen before. "Fine, friend. Keep it." Her eyes stay on him a beat longer than a dealer's usually stay on a man who's said no, and then the family with the handcart is level with her crate and she's calling to them instead.

The arch is cool and smells of old stone and mule. On the far side the Lower City opens up and drops toward the harbour in roofs and chimney smoke. The notice board is fixed to the inner face of the gatehouse wall, just past the arch, where the street lamp hasn't been lit yet. The cat goes ahead of James without being asked and sits down under it.

Up close, the card is smaller than it looked from the queue, about the size of a good deck's cards, maybe a little taller. The ivory has fine grain lines running down it like the rings in wood, and the edges are bevelled by hand. The paint has crazed in places with tiny cracks, the way old varnish cracks. This card wasn't made this year, or in this lifetime. The iron tack through the top margin is new, though. Its head is bright and unrusted, while the tacks holding up the wanted poster beside it have bled orange streaks down the paper. Whoever put the card up did it within the last few days.

The woman's veil is painted so thin you can see both faces through it. The smiling one has warm colour in her cheeks. The profile turned away is done in cooler tones, grey-green and shadowed, and painted just as carefully. Nobody hurried it. The coin between her fingers is a single stroke of gold leaf, edge-on, a line and nothing more.

James knows this part without anyone telling him. Every priest of the Lady tells it sooner or later, usually over the second cup. Before there were two sisters there was one goddess, Tyche, and she was broken in two. Tymora got the smile. Beshaba got the rest. Most temples of the Lady don't like to paint that story, and none of them paint it like this.

As he leans in, the Coin of Tymora at his throat goes cold again. This time it stays cold, a small cold disc against his breastbone, as long as he stands within arm's reach of the board.

The cat isn't looking at the whole card now. It's looking up at the turned-away face, the grey-green profile. Its tail is wrapped tight around its paws and it doesn't blink.

From here the back of the card is out of sight, flat against the wood. There's only the single tack and a margin of yellowed ivory where a thumbnail could get underneath.

Out past the arch, the crate by the roadside still stands where it was, but the cards are gone from it. So is Tamsin Reed.

James slides a thumbnail under the top margin and takes the card's weight on two fingers, so it can't drop when the tack comes free. The tack is new and the board is soft pine, and it comes out with one slow pull and no sound. The card settles onto his fingertips. It weighs almost nothing, less than a silver piece.

He turns it over.

The back is plain ivory, darker with age than the face, and right in the middle of it is a seal of two interlocked circles. They weren't painted on. Someone cut them into the ivory with a fine graver and filled the grooves, one circle with gold and the other with something dark that might once have been silver and has gone black. The circles cross in two places. At one crossing the gold ring lies over the dark one, and at the other the dark ring lies over the gold. Whoever cut it did that on purpose, so neither ring is on top. Where the two circles overlap, in the narrow almond of shared space between them, the ivory is worn smooth and faintly hollowed, as if a great many thumbs have rubbed that spot over a great many years.

The seal is as old as the face. The writing under it is new.

Across the bottom margin, in brown-black ink that hasn't faded at all, someone has written in a cramped hand that doesn't waste letters:

*Mermaid. Rope-cellar. Midnight, any night to the dark of the moon. Ask for Hollis.*

That's all of it. There's no signature, no job and no price. Whoever wrote it didn't think the right reader would need any of those.

With the face turned down against his palm, the painted side feels warm, warm as skin, warmer than his own hand. At the same time the Coin of Tymora is a disc of cold against his breastbone, colder now than it was. For a moment he feels both at once, the warmth in his hand and the cold at his throat, and neither gives way to the other.

At his feet the cat has stopped watching the card. It's looking up at James, tail still wrapped tight, eyes steady, waiting.

Behind him, under the arch, Vask's flat voice is still working through the queue. "Name. Business." The sergeant hasn't turned around. Nobody on the street seems to care that a card has come off the board. Somebody lights the street lamp above the board with a long pole and a grunt and moves on to the next one.

James is holding the card in one hand and the bright little tack in the other.

James has no paper or ink of his own, but the board has plenty of paper. A curfew notice from last spring hangs in rags at the bottom, and its blank lower half tears away cleanly. Above his head the street lamp has just been lit and is still smoking, and the glass has a fresh ring of soot round the top. He wipes the point of the tack through it and writes. The letters come out grey and smudgy, but every word is there: *Mermaid. Rope-cellar. Midnight, any night to the dark of the moon. Ask for Hollis.* He folds the strip once and puts it away.

*(Aside: your sheet lists no paper or writing kit, so I used what was to hand at the board. If you'd rather he'd done it another way, tell me.)*

Then he puts the card back. Face out, the same height, the tack through the same tiny hole in the top margin, so the painted woman doesn't get a second wound. The pine takes the tack as easily as it gave it up. When his fingers leave the ivory, the warmth leaves his palm. A breath later the Coin of Tymora at his throat loses its chill and goes back to being his own temperature, like any coin worn against the skin.

"Wouldn't want the next guest missing the invitation."

The cat looks at the card one more time, at the smiling face this time, not the one turned away. Then its tail comes loose from around its paws and it stands up, stretches the long way cats do, and goes down the street ahead of him.

The Lower City pours downhill from the gate. The streets are narrow and steep and noisy with shutters going up for the evening trade or coming down for the night. Cookfires and fish are in the air, and under them, from farther down, wet rope and tar. Halfway down the first street a woman is wrestling a shutter over a shop window full of tallow candles and coils of wick. She's sixty or so, broad in the shoulders, with her sleeves pushed up past the elbow. A painted board over her door reads *COYLE — CHANDLER — LAMP OIL*.

She hears the question before he's finished it and doesn't stop working the shutter bolt.

"The Mermaid." She gives the bolt a shove with the heel of her hand. "You're not buying anything, are you? No. Then it's quick." She points down the hill with her chin. "Keep going down till you can't go down any more. That's the water. Turn left along the quays, past the fish sheds. You'll know them, you'll smell them. Past the ropewalk. Then there's a house with a red door and a mermaid over it, and the paint on her's gone so pink she looks like she's been at the gin." She snorts at that. "That's the one. You'll hear it before you see it."

Then she looks at him properly: the good coat, the purse, the cat sitting on her doorstep as if it's been invited.

"Keep that purse inside your coat down there. And if anyone in the Mermaid offers you work, ask what it is first. Half of them won't tell you, and that's your answer." The bolt catches. "Evening."

The door shuts, and a moment later her lamp goes out behind the shutters.

Her directions are good. The street ends at a wall of masts and black water with the last red light on it. To the left the fish sheds stink just as she promised. Then comes the ropewalk, a long, low shed where two boys are coiling the day's cable by lamplight. Past it, maybe a hundred feet farther along the quay, there's a red door under a carved mermaid whose paint has faded to the pink of a drunkard's cheeks. The windows are yellow and fogged. Someone inside is singing badly and three other people are singing worse. Out front a pair of dockhands share a pipe and don't look up.

It's not yet eight bells. Midnight is more than four hours off.

The cat sits down at the edge of the quay, between James and the door, and waits for him.

James buttons the purse inside his coat before he touches the red door. The two dockhands out front watch him do it and go back to their pipe.

Inside, the Mermaid is low, hot and loud. The ceiling beams are black with years of pipe smoke, and the floor is sanded boards gone grey with spilled beer. The singers are three sailors in a corner booth with a fourth asleep across the table. All of them have forgotten the second verse and keep singing the first one again. There are maybe thirty people in the room: dockhands, a few sailors with salt-white rings on their boots, two women in good wool counting something under the table, and a ring of men on their knees by the hearth throwing dice against the wall. Every throw gets a shout.

The bar runs along the left wall. The woman behind it is built like a mooring post. She has grey hair cropped short and an old burn scar shining on one forearm, and she's wiping a mug that won't get any cleaner. She hears the order without looking up.

"Stew's eel and barley. Ale's what there is." She fills a mug from the cask behind her and puts it in front of him. "A silver the pair."

When he puts the coin down she takes it and shouts "Bowl!" through a door behind her. Then she looks at him properly. She takes in the coat, the face, and the cat, which has jumped onto the stool beside him and sits there like a paying customer.

"Room's five silver. Bed, a door, a bolt that works. Two silver gets you the floor upstairs with whoever else is on it." She jerks her chin at the cat. "That one stays off my bar."

While he waits, James gets the shape of the place.

The red door behind him is the front way, onto the quay. The kitchen door is behind the bar, open, and through it comes steam and the smell of eel. Past the kitchen a second door stands on the latch, and cold air off an alley comes in under it. A narrow stair in the back corner climbs to the rooms. The windows are small, fogged and set high. A man could get through one, but not quickly.

The fourth way out is at the far end of the bar, where the room goes dim. It's a low door with iron bands across it, and a dozen coils of old rope hang on pegs beside it like a sign. A broad man sits on a stool by the door, whittling something small. He hasn't once looked up at the singing. Every time the kitchen door swings, though, he looks at it.

The cat has stopped watching the room. It's looking at a table near the hearth, at the edge of the dice game, where an old man sits alone. He has a long boathook leaning against the wall beside him, its iron worn bright. There's a stone jar on the table in front of him, stoppered with a cork, and one big, scarred hand rests on top of it as if someone might take it. He drinks with the other hand. The cat's tail is wrapped tight around its paws.

A boy comes out of the kitchen with a bowl of something brown and steaming and sets it down beside the ale with a spoon stuck upright in it.

The barkeep is still waiting, cloth in hand.

"Room or floor, or neither? I don't hold beds past nine bells."

Marta takes the five silver without counting it twice. She drops it under the bar, and the name goes past her the way the singing does.

"Didn't ask." A key on a loop of tarred cord lands on the wood. "Top of the stair, second door. The bolt's on the inside. Out by noon, or you pay another night."

"Off you come." The cat drops from the stool without a sound. Marta watches it all the way to the floor, as if she expected it to try the bar on the way.

James carries the bowl and the mug across the room. The dice ring by the hearth throws, and someone groans and someone else laughs and slaps the wall. Just past the edge of all that, the old man sits in a pocket of quiet. Up close he's bigger than he looked, with heavy shoulders gone round with age, and forearms roped with scars from wire or rope or both. He smells of river mud, tar and old wet wool. James sets his bowl down at the far end of the table, with an arm's length of scarred wood between it and the stone jar.

The old man doesn't answer right away. He looks at James for a long moment, at his face and coat and hands, with pale, red-rimmed eyes that don't hurry. Then he looks down at the cat. It has settled under the bench with its tail wrapped tight, staring up at the jar.

"Chair's not mine." His voice is low and rough, like it isn't used often. He drinks. His other hand doesn't move off the cork. "Sit, if you're sitting."

James sits. For a while it's just the stew, which is better than it looks: eel, barley, too much salt and a lot of pepper to cover it.

The old man is watching the cat again.

"Your cat's been at my jar since you came through the door." It isn't a complaint, just a fact he's noting. "Can't have it."

Then his eyes lift and stop at James's throat, at the cord and the small disc of the Coin of Tymora where his collar has fallen open. His scarred fingers close a little tighter around the top of the jar.

"That a coin you've got round your neck?"

"So she had someone follow us." James looks down at the six of cups on the grey blanket. "We'll leave her waiting for a change."

He picks it up by the edges and slips it into the outer pocket of his coat, on the opposite side from his own deck. The two shouldn't touch.

At the window the cat pulls its head back in from the gap. For a moment it stays on the ledge, still looking uphill, before it steps down onto the bed. James takes the stool out of the shutter and the leather hinge swings the shutter closed on the alley. The midden smell stays in the room a while longer than the cold does.

After that he just waits.

The waiting is long. The straw rustles whenever he shifts his weight. The rushlight on the landing burns down and somebody replaces it, because the line under the door goes dark, then comes back brighter and steadier. Nobody stops outside. Under the floor the argument that replaced the singers has burned itself out, and the room has settled into the low steady mutter of a tavern that won't close so much as run out of customers. The dice ring breaks up some time after ten. Eleven bells come up off the water, and later the half after eleven. Somebody goes up the stair heavily, laughing at nothing, and bangs the first door shut. It's a drunk, nothing like the earlier footsteps, and the cat barely lifts its head.

Shortly after the quarter before midnight James gets up off the bed. He checks that the rapier sits right in its scabbard, buttons the purse inside his coat and draws the bolt as quietly as iron allows.

The cat has stood up on the blanket. It's facing him, not the door.

*Wait here. I'll come back for you.*

It holds his eye for a breath. Then it lies down again in the hollow his body left in the straw, wraps its tail tight around its paws and turns to face the door. It stays that way while he steps out and pulls the door shut behind him. The key turns in the lock from outside.

The taproom has thinned to perhaps a dozen people. The singers are gone. The fourth man was carried out or woke and walked out, and their booth is a wreck of mugs. Two sailors are asleep upright by the cold end of the hearth. Somebody is playing a slow game of knucklebones alone, a few old men are finishing their last cups, and a dockhand stands at the bar with his head in his hands. Marta is wiping down the far end of the bar and doesn't look up as he passes. Garrow's table by the hearth is empty.

At the dim end of the room the broad man is still on his stool beside the iron-banded door. The little fish in his hand has more scales now, and the pile of shavings on his knee has grown. He finishes the scale he's on. Then he looks up at James, past him toward the stair, and down at the empty floor by James's heel.

He gives a small nod, as if James has got the first part right.

Midnight comes up off the quay one stroke at a time, slow and wet, the sound carrying in under the red door. The doorman waits for the last of the twelve strokes. Then he sets the knife and the fish down on the stool, stands, and knocks on the black door with the side of his fist: two knocks, a pause, one more.

For a while nothing happens. James can hear the sleeping sailors breathing, and the knucklebones clicking on the table behind him.

Then there's a voice from beyond the door, below it and a long way down, as if it has come up a stair. It's a man's voice, dry and unhurried.

"Who's asking?"

"Card reader." The doorman keeps his own voice low and never takes his eyes off James. "Read it at the gate. Put it back after. Came in tonight, sat with the hook-man, came to me first and asked how it's done."

The silence below goes on longer this time.

"The one with the cat?"

The doorman's eyes flick to the empty floor again. "Left it upstairs."

Somewhere below, something small is set down on wood.

"Yes," the voice says. "Send him down."

The doorman takes a key from inside his smock, iron and as long as a hand, and fits it into the big keyhole. The lock turns with a sound like a heavy drawer closing. He pulls the door open toward himself. Cold air comes out, smelling of tarred hemp, wet stone and lamp oil. Beyond the door a narrow stair goes down between brick walls, each step worn hollow in the middle. A single lamp burns at the bottom, below the curve of the wall where James can't see.

The doorman stands aside with the door in his hand.

"Blade stays sheathed. Hands where he can see them." He looks James over one last time, quickly, the way he looked at him at nine. "I'm up here the whole time."

He holds the door and waits.

I tuck my purse inside my coat before entering the Mermaid. At the bar, I order a bowl of stew and an ale, and ask, “What do you charge for a room tonight?” While I wait, I take in the room and its exits.

“Room.” I count out five silver. “James Worgen.”

With a quiet “Off you come” to the cat, I carry my supper over to the old man's table, leaving room between me and his jar.

“Mind some company? I've spent the day on the road, and this one”—I nod at the cat—“isn't much for conversation.”

“Aye. Tymora's.” I lift it clear of my collar without taking it off. “A reminder of a promise.”

I glance down at the cat. “Leave his jar alone.”

Then back to the old man. “You recognised it. Mean something to you?”

“Following a lead, though I don't yet know where it ends. An ivory card at the gate said to come here and ask for Hollis at midnight.”

I lower the coin back against my shirt.

“I can't tell you why the cat noticed your jar. But men turning up dead with coins under their tongues deserves better than a shrug and another drink. Have you kept one of those coins?”

“Beshaba,” I say quietly, keeping my voice at our table. “Not Umberlee. Someone's marking these dead for the Maid of Misfortune.”

I leave the coppers untouched.

“Were they drowned, Garrow, or dead before they reached the water? And where did you find the most recent one?”

“I'll ask what they know. Carefully—and without putting your name to it.”

I finish my ale. “If I need to find you again, where should I look? And who at the dead-house took the man with the ring?”

I take my empty bowl and mug back to the bar, then approach the man whittling beside the rope-hung door.

“Evening. I'm here to see Hollis at midnight. Do I speak to you when the time comes?”

“Off the back of an ivory card pinned by the gate. Two-faced lady on the front, gold and dark circles on the back.”

I keep my voice as low as his. “I put it back when I'd read it.”

“Midnight, then.”

I head upstairs with the cat, check my room, and bolt the door behind us. I settle on the bed to rest until shortly before midnight, leaving enough time to return downstairs for the bells.
I rest with the cat beside me, listening for the quay bells so I don't miss midnight.

Without opening the door, I send the cat a quiet mental instruction: *Follow whoever just left. Keep your distance. Don't confront them.*

I let it out of the shutter onto the alley side to make its way back through the kitchen, then lie still behind the bolted door and look through its eyes.
I keep watching through the cat's eyes as it tries to pick up the listener's scent, leaving it to choose a quiet route inside.

Before the link fades, I send one last instruction: *Follow him quietly. See where he goes and who he meets, but don't enter anywhere you can't easily escape. Then come back to our room.*

I release the borrowed senses and open the shutter enough for the cat to return, then wait beside it.

I crouch beside the cat and hold out a hand for it to sniff.

*Good work. Did he meet the woman dealing cards at the gate?* I picture her face as I ask through our bond. *Can you show me—or help me understand—where he stopped?*

I let the cat respond without pressing it, leaving the marked six on the blanket.

“So she had someone follow us.” I glance at the marked six. “We'll leave her waiting for a change.”

I tuck the card into an outer pocket, away from my own deck, and let the cat back inside before closing the shutter. I stay in the bolted room until a few minutes before midnight, then head down to the doorman, leaving the cat resting on the bed.

*Wait here. I'll come back for you.*

The atmosphere worked very well. The gate queue, Garrow’s muddy coat, Marta’s room key, the doorman carving his fish—all gave me people and places I could picture and respond to. Refusing the card game felt like a meaningful character choice without making James’s weakness take over the opening. Taking down the ivory card, reading it, and putting it back also felt like a choice the world noticed.

Garrow was the strongest scene for me. His concern gave James a reason to care beyond “my goddess sent me,” and the missing ring and false Fist attendant were concrete clues worth investigating. I also appreciated having time to eat, secure a room, learn the entrances, and approach the midnight meeting on my own terms.

What broke or dragged:
- **The opening was very slow.** We spent the whole session reaching the door of the first substantial meeting. I’d have preferred to meet Hollis and hear the initial proposition before the cutoff.
- **Raw tool-call markup appeared in the narration**, including a supposedly private watcher roll. That exposed information James didn’t know and interrupted the scene.
- **Some rules and numbers were inconsistent.** Perception was rolled at +2 despite the sheet’s +1; Healing Light was capped at four dice rather than the campaign sheet’s five. A quick reconciliation at the start would help.
- The repeated descriptions—tails wrapped tightly, slow wet bells, dice hitting the wall, people testing words “like a rope”—became noticeable. They were evocative initially, but repetition stretched scenes.

What I missed was an early sense of the campaign’s promised crew-and-heist direction. The mysteries are interesting, but I’m still waiting to learn what James might actually be asked to do. A concrete offer would give me something to plan around.

Overall, I wanted to keep playing. Keep the grounded NPCs, consequences, and investigable clues; compress uneventful waiting and repeated atmosphere, and let the first session deliver a clear proposition alongside the mystery.

Yes—when the cat came back with the marked six and pointed toward the gate, I wanted to go find Tamsin and confront her about having James followed.

I stayed because midnight had been established as the important appointment, and I didn’t know whether a trip uphill would make me miss it. I also wanted to reach Hollis before the session ended. That was partly James being cautious, partly me protecting our progress toward the main hook.

The temptation worked: I was genuinely curious about Tamsin. What held me back was pacing and uncertainty about travel time, rather than a lack of interest.

turns.reply:
James doesn't step out of the line. The dealer laughs, quick and bright, and her hands never stop moving.

"Then she's smiling at the wrong man, friend. I'm the one she's paying tonight." She fans the deck, closes it, and fans it again. "Offer stands while the line does."

James looks past her, past the dwarf's mule, to the notice board. It's maybe thirty feet away, close to forty, half in the long shadow of the arch. The cat hasn't moved. Its tail is wrapped tight around its paws.

The cart ahead rolls forward, and the last of the sun slips under the arch and strikes the board at a low angle. For a moment James sees the card clearly.

It isn't pasteboard. Pasteboard curls and goes soft at the corners in the damp off the river, and this card hasn't. It hangs flat and stiff and has a faint yellowish sheen, like old bone or ivory, thin enough that the light almost comes through at the edges. Someone painted it by hand. James has held thousands of cards, and no printer's block makes lines that fine.

The face shows a woman in a veil, and she has two faces under it. One looks straight out at the street, smiling. The other is turned away in profile, so all you see is a cheek and the line of a jaw, as if she's listening to someone behind her. She holds a coin up between finger and thumb, edge-on to the viewer, so you can't tell which side is up. There's no suit and no number on it, and no word or price on it anywhere. Whoever pinned it put a single iron tack through the top margin and kept it carefully clear of the painting.

James has played a good many decks between Tethyr and the Sword Coast, and he has never seen this card in any of them.

Then the light is gone. In the same moment the Coin of Tymora at his throat goes cold against his skin, the way a coin feels when it has just come out of someone else's hand. It lasts the space of a breath, and then it's just metal warmed by his own body again.

The cat still hasn't looked away from the card.

"Next." The sergeant turns a page in his ledger without looking up. One traveller is left between James and the arch: the dwarf, who is now arguing with his mule about whether it will walk under the stone.

The dwarf gets his mule under the arch with a slap on the rump and a word that makes the family behind him cover a child's ears. Then the sergeant is in front of James. He's a heavy man in a faded red tabard, with ink on two fingers and a ledger that has seen too many hands today.

"James Worgen," the sergeant repeats, and writes it down. His letters are square and slow. "Lodgings and work. As long as it holds." He writes that too, word for word, as if he's heard it a thousand times.

His eyes go to the cat for a moment, then to the purse at James's belt. The pen stops. Beside the entry, in the margin, he makes a small mark, a short slanted stroke, and then he's writing again as if he never paused.

At the question about the board he doesn't look round.

"Not Fist business." He blots the line. "Board-man takes a copper, anything goes up. Cards go up now and then. Lower City business. They're for somebody." Now he does look up, flat and tired. "Somebody's not usually the man asking."

Off to the side, Tamsin has stopped dealing. She doesn't pretend she wasn't listening.

"He's right, friend, it's not a lost-and-found." She taps the top of her deck with one finger. "But I know what it says on the back. One hand and I'll tell you. Win or lose, you still get your answer."

The sergeant ignores her, the way you ignore a fly that's been there all day. He turns the ledger a quarter-turn and holds out his ink-stained hand, palm up.

"Gate toll's a silver. Animal's another two." The cat hasn't moved its eyes from the notice board. "Three silver, and you're in."

Sergeant Vask's ink-stained hand closes around the gold piece. He doesn't bite it or even look at it. He drops it into a dented tin box at his elbow and counts the change out of the same tin, one silver at a time, onto James's palm.

"Seven." He's already looking past James's shoulder. "In. Next."

Behind him, Tamsin's cards go on whispering on the crate.

"A promise." She says it lightly, like a trick she's seen before. "Fine, friend. Keep it." Her eyes stay on him a beat longer than a dealer's usually stay on a man who's said no, and then the family with the handcart is level with her crate and she's calling to them instead.

The arch is cool and smells of old stone and mule. On the far side the Lower City opens up and drops toward the harbour in roofs and chimney smoke. The notice board is fixed to the inner face of the gatehouse wall, just past the arch, where the street lamp hasn't been lit yet. The cat goes ahead of James without being asked and sits down under it.

Up close, the card is smaller than it looked from the queue, about the size of a good deck's cards, maybe a little taller. The ivory has fine grain lines running down it like the rings in wood, and the edges are bevelled by hand. The paint has crazed in places with tiny cracks, the way old varnish cracks. This card wasn't made this year, or in this lifetime. The iron tack through the top margin is new, though. Its head is bright and unrusted, while the tacks holding up the wanted poster beside it have bled orange streaks down the paper. Whoever put the card up did it within the last few days.

The woman's veil is painted so thin you can see both faces through it. The smiling one has warm colour in her cheeks. The profile turned away is done in cooler tones, grey-green and shadowed, and painted just as carefully. Nobody hurried it. The coin between her fingers is a single stroke of gold leaf, edge-on, a line and nothing more.

James knows this part without anyone telling him. Every priest of the Lady tells it sooner or later, usually over the second cup. Before there were two sisters there was one goddess, Tyche, and she was broken in two. Tymora got the smile. Beshaba got the rest. Most temples of the Lady don't like to paint that story, and none of them paint it like this.

As he leans in, the Coin of Tymora at his throat goes cold again. This time it stays cold, a small cold disc against his breastbone, as long as he stands within arm's reach of the board.

The cat isn't looking at the whole card now. It's looking up at the turned-away face, the grey-green profile. Its tail is wrapped tight around its paws and it doesn't blink.

From here the back of the card is out of sight, flat against the wood. There's only the single tack and a margin of yellowed ivory where a thumbnail could get underneath.

Out past the arch, the crate by the roadside still stands where it was, but the cards are gone from it. So is Tamsin Reed.

James slides a thumbnail under the top margin and takes the card's weight on two fingers, so it can't drop when the tack comes free. The tack is new and the board is soft pine, and it comes out with one slow pull and no sound. The card settles onto his fingertips. It weighs almost nothing, less than a silver piece.

He turns it over.

The back is plain ivory, darker with age than the face, and right in the middle of it is a seal of two interlocked circles. They weren't painted on. Someone cut them into the ivory with a fine graver and filled the grooves, one circle with gold and the other with something dark that might once have been silver and has gone black. The circles cross in two places. At one crossing the gold ring lies over the dark one, and at the other the dark ring lies over the gold. Whoever cut it did that on purpose, so neither ring is on top. Where the two circles overlap, in the narrow almond of shared space between them, the ivory is worn smooth and faintly hollowed, as if a great many thumbs have rubbed that spot over a great many years.

The seal is as old as the face. The writing under it is new.

Across the bottom margin, in brown-black ink that hasn't faded at all, someone has written in a cramped hand that doesn't waste letters:

*Mermaid. Rope-cellar. Midnight, any night to the dark of the moon. Ask for Hollis.*

That's all of it. There's no signature, no job and no price. Whoever wrote it didn't think the right reader would need any of those.

With the face turned down against his palm, the painted side feels warm, warm as skin, warmer than his own hand. At the same time the Coin of Tymora is a disc of cold against his breastbone, colder now than it was. For a moment he feels both at once, the warmth in his hand and the cold at his throat, and neither gives way to the other.

At his feet the cat has stopped watching the card. It's looking up at James, tail still wrapped tight, eyes steady, waiting.

Behind him, under the arch, Vask's flat voice is still working through the queue. "Name. Business." The sergeant hasn't turned around. Nobody on the street seems to care that a card has come off the board. Somebody lights the street lamp above the board with a long pole and a grunt and moves on to the next one.

Above his head the street lamp has just been lit and is still smoking, and the glass has a fresh ring of soot round the top. He wipes the point of the tack through it and writes. The letters come out grey and smudgy, but every word is there: *Mermaid. Rope-cellar. Midnight, any night to the dark of the moon. Ask for Hollis.* He folds the strip once and puts it away.

*(Aside: your sheet lists no paper or writing kit, so I used what was to hand at the board. If you'd rather he'd done it another way, tell me.)*

Then he puts the card back. Face out, the same height, the tack through the same tiny hole in the top margin, so the painted woman doesn't get a second wound. The pine takes the tack as easily as it gave it up. When his fingers leave the ivory, the warmth leaves his palm. A breath later the Coin of Tymora at his throat loses its chill and goes back to being his own temperature, like any coin worn against the skin.

"Wouldn't want the next guest missing the invitation."

The cat looks at the card one more time, at the smiling face this time, not the one turned away. Then its tail comes loose from around its paws and it stands up, stretches the long way cats do, and goes down the street ahead of him.

The Lower City pours downhill from the gate. The streets are narrow and steep and noisy with shutters going up for the evening trade or coming down for the night. Cookfires and fish are in the air, and under them, from farther down, wet rope and tar. Halfway down the first street a woman is wrestling a shutter over a shop window full of tallow candles and coils of wick. She's sixty or so, broad in the shoulders, with her sleeves pushed up past the elbow. A painted board over her door reads *COYLE — CHANDLER — LAMP OIL*.

She hears the question before he's finished it and doesn't stop working the shutter bolt.

"The Mermaid." She gives the bolt a shove with the heel of her hand. "You're not buying anything, are you? No. Then it's quick." She points down the hill with her chin. "Keep going down till you can't go down any more. That's the water. Turn left along the quays, past the fish sheds. You'll know them, you'll smell them. Past the ropewalk. Then there's a house with a red door and a mermaid over it, and the paint on her's gone so pink she looks like she's been at the gin." She snorts at that. "That's the one. You'll hear it before you see it."

Then she looks at him properly: the good coat, the purse, the cat sitting on her doorstep as if it's been invited.

"Keep that purse inside your coat down there. And if anyone in the Mermaid offers you work, ask what it is first. Half of them won't tell you, and that's your answer." The bolt catches. "Evening."

The door shuts, and a moment later her lamp goes out behind the shutters.

Her directions are good. The street ends at a wall of masts and black water with the last red light on it. To the left the fish sheds stink just as she promised. Then comes the ropewalk, a long, low shed where two boys are coiling the day's cable by lamplight. Past it, maybe a hundred feet farther along the quay, there's a red door under a carved mermaid whose paint has faded to the pink of a drunkard's cheeks. The windows are yellow and fogged. Someone inside is singing badly and three other people are singing worse. Out front a pair of dockhands share a pipe and don't look up.

It's not yet eight bells. Midnight is more than four hours off.

The cat sits down at the edge of the quay, between James and the door, and waits for him.

Inside, the Mermaid is low, hot and loud. The ceiling beams are black with years of pipe smoke, and the floor is sanded boards gone grey with spilled beer. The singers are three sailors in a corner booth with a fourth asleep across the table. All of them have forgotten the second verse and keep singing the first one again. There are maybe thirty people in the room: dockhands, a few sailors with salt-white rings on their boots, two women in good wool counting something under the table, and a ring of men on their knees by the hearth throwing dice against the wall. Every throw gets a shout.

The bar runs along the left wall. The woman behind it is built like a mooring post. She has grey hair cropped short and an old burn scar shining on one forearm, and she's wiping a mug that won't get any cleaner. She hears the order without looking up.

"Stew's eel and barley. Ale's what there is." She fills a mug from the cask behind her and puts it in front of him. "A silver the pair."

When he puts the coin down she takes it and shouts "Bowl!" through a door behind her. Then she looks at him properly. She takes in the coat, the face, and the cat, which has jumped onto the stool beside him and sits there like a paying customer.

"Room's five silver. Bed, a door, a bolt that works. Two silver gets you the floor upstairs with whoever else is on it." She jerks her chin at the cat. "That one stays off my bar."

“Room.” I count out five silver. “James Worgen.”

With a quiet “Off you come” to the cat, I carry my supper over to the old man's table, leaving room between me and his jar.

“Mind some company? I've spent the day on the road, and this one”—I nod at the cat—“isn't much for conversation.”

"Didn't ask." A key on a loop of tarred cord lands on the wood. "Top of the stair, second door. The bolt's on the inside. Out by noon, or you pay another night."

"Off you come." The cat drops from the stool without a sound. Marta watches it all the way to the floor, as if she expected it to try the bar on the way.

James carries the bowl and the mug across the room. The dice ring by the hearth throws, and someone groans and someone else laughs and slaps the wall. Just past the edge of all that, the old man sits in a pocket of quiet. Up close he's bigger than he looked, with heavy shoulders gone round with age, and forearms roped with scars from wire or rope or both. He smells of river mud, tar and old wet wool. James sets his bowl down at the far end of the table, with an arm's length of scarred wood between it and the stone jar.

The old man doesn't answer right away. He looks at James for a long moment, at his face and coat and hands, with pale, red-rimmed eyes that don't hurry. Then he looks down at the cat. It has settled under the bench with its tail wrapped tight, staring up at the jar.

"Chair's not mine." His voice is low and rough, like it isn't used often. He drinks. His other hand doesn't move off the cork. "Sit, if you're sitting."

James sits. For a while it's just the stew, which is better than it looks: eel, barley, too much salt and a lot of pepper to cover it.

The old man is watching the cat again.

"Your cat's been at my jar since you came through the door." It isn't a complaint, just a fact he's noting. "Can't have it."

Then his eyes lift and stop at James's throat, at the cord and the small disc of the Coin of Tymora where his collar has fallen open. His scarred fingers close a little tighter around the top of the jar.

"Leave his jar alone."

"Not that face." He says it slowly, as if he's checking it against something. "Wanted to see the face."

He drinks, puts the mug down and wipes his mouth with the back of his wrist. His other hand stays where it is on the jar.

"I work the harbour. Hook and a skiff. Anything goes in the water between the Seatower and the fish sheds, I bring it out. Mostly it's the dead." He nods at the boathook against the wall without looking at it. "Thirty years of it, near enough."

He leans in a little over the scarred wood. Up close the smell of river mud is stronger.

"Lately some of them come up with a coin in the mouth. Under the tongue, where you'd put it yourself if you meant it to stay." He's watching James's face the whole time, not the coin now. "Folk on the quay say it's the sea's fare. Say it and go on drinking. Nobody asks who's paying it."

His thumb moves once across the cork, and then it's still.

turns.message:
“Following a lead, though I don't yet know where it ends. An ivory card at the gate said to come here and ask for Hollis at midnight.”

I lower the coin back against my shirt.

“I can't tell you why the cat noticed your jar. But men turning up dead with coins under their tongues deserves better than a shrug and another drink. Have you kept one of those coins?”
turns.reply:
The old man watches the coin go back under James's shirt. Then he looks at James's face for a long time, the way he looked at the coin, and the dice hit the wall twice before he answers.

"Rope-cellar's the Guild's door." He doesn't look toward the far end of the bar, where the broad man sits whittling. "Men go down there with nothing and come up with work. Some come up with money. I don't know any Hollis. Don't want to."

He drinks, and sets the mug down carefully.

"Better than a shrug." He says it over to himself, flat, as if he's testing whether a rope will hold. Then he slides the boathook a little closer along the wall with his elbow, leans his body between the table and the dice ring, and works the cork out of the jar with his thumb.

He doesn't hand the jar over. He tips it, and a small dull heap of copper slides out under the cup of his big palm, where nobody behind him can see it. He spreads the coins with one finger.

There are seventeen of them. Some are bright where the water has scoured them, and some have gone green. All of them are coppers, ordinary city coppers by their size and weight, and on every one of them someone has filed one face down until it's smooth. The duke or the ship or whatever was struck there is gone. On the other face, pressed in with a punch and filled black, is a small mark the size of a fingernail: a pair of antlers.

James doesn't need anyone to tell him what it is. Every priest of the Lady knows that mark, and so does every gambler who ever sat at a table with one. Black antlers are the sign of Beshaba, the Maid of Misfortune, the sister you don't name over the dice. Umberlee's priestesses use a wave, and they want their offerings thrown into the sea, not put under a dead man's tongue. Whoever paid this fare wasn't paying the sea.

Against James's breastbone the Coin of Tymora stays exactly as warm as his skin. It doesn't go cold the way it did at the gate. These are just coppers, filed and punched by somebody's hand.

Under the bench the cat hasn't moved from his boot, but its head has come round from the hearth and it's looking at the little heap of copper. It doesn't blink.

"Seventeen since the thaw." The old man's finger rests on the greenest one. "Before that, none. Thirty years, and none." He pushes them back together into a heap with the side of his hand. "They call me Garrow on the quay. I put them in the jar because nobody else would take them out of the dead men's mouths."

His pale eyes come up to James's face again. His other hand is back on the jar's mouth.

"You know that mark." It isn't really a question, the way he says it, but he waits for an answer all the same.

turns.message:
“Beshaba,” I say quietly, keeping my voice at our table. “Not Umberlee. Someone's marking these dead for the Maid of Misfortune.”

I leave the coppers untouched.

“Were they drowned, Garrow, or dead before they reached the water? And where did you find the most recent one?”
turns.reply:
The dice hit the wall behind them and the ring by the hearth roars. Garrow doesn't turn round. He watches James say the name, and after that he watches James's hands, which stay flat on the table well away from the copper.

Something in the old man's shoulders lets go a little. He pushes the coins back into the jar with the side of his palm. They make almost no sound against the stone, and he works the cork home with his thumb.

"Beshaba." He says it low, as if trying how it sounds. "Quay says Umberlee. Easier, I suppose. You can pay Umberlee off."

He drinks before he answers the rest.

"Drowned. Alive when they went in. There's froth in the mouth and water in the chest. Thirty years, I know a drowned man." He turns the mug a quarter-turn on the wood. "But they didn't fight it. A man who goes in at night fights. Torn nails, splinters off the piles, skin off his knuckles. These come up clean. Hands open. Like they lay down in it."

He lets that sit.

"Last one was two nights back. West side of the Seatower causeway, where the tide piles everything against the stones. Young. Soft hands, so he wasn't off the docks. Good boots. Nobody's come asking." He shrugs one heavy shoulder. "Nobody comes for any of them."

Under the bench the cat hasn't moved off James's boot. Now that the jar is corked it looks at the cork instead, as if the coppers were still lying in plain sight.

Garrow is quiet long enough that James thinks he's finished. Then he leans in again, lower, so the smell of river mud comes with him.

"Last month there was one with a ring. Silver, a seal on it. I didn't take it. I don't take off the dead, only the copper." His big hand settles back over the jar. "A seal with a ship and three stars. That's Thalendar. Factors wear it, the men who keep their books on the wharves. Their ships berth at the long pier past the Seatower, and they always have."

He sits back.

"I took him to the Fist dead-house, same as the rest. Next day I asked. The ring wasn't on the list. He went in the paupers' ground with no name on him." He looks at the far end of the bar, at the iron-banded door and the broad man whittling beside it, and then back at James. "A patriar house loses its own man. It doesn't come for him. It doesn't come for his ring."

The singers in the corner have finally found the second verse and are murdering it. Garrow's red-rimmed eyes stay on James's face.

"You're going down there at midnight. To this Hollis." It isn't quite a question. "Men down there know what's moving on the water before the water does."

Marta looks up when the empty bowl and mug land on her bar. It's plain from her face that nobody brings them back. She takes them in one hand, sends them through the kitchen door without turning round, and goes back to her mug.

At the far end of the bar the room gets darker, a few steps at a time, and the noise of the dice ring fades behind James. Close to, the coils of rope on the pegs aren't for decoration. They're old cable, gone hard with tar and salt, every coil hung the same way, like a rule nobody has written down. The door they hang beside is low and black. Its iron bands are worn bright at hand height, and the keyhole is big enough for a man's thumb.

The man on the stool is broader up close and younger than he looked, maybe thirty. He has a flattened nose and forearms like a dock porter's. A short cudgel wrapped in leather leans against the leg of his stool, where his heel could find it without him looking. The thing in his hand is a small wooden fish, about as long as a finger. He's cutting scales into it one at a time with the tip of a short knife, and the shavings collect on his knee.

He hears James out and finishes the scale he's on before he looks up. His eyes are dark and patient. They go over James once, the coat, the hands, the rapier, and then down to the cat, which has stopped a pace behind James's heel and sits there looking at the iron-banded door, not at the man.

"Midnight." He says it as if he's checking it against something. "Yeah. You come to me. Not before."

The kitchen door swings behind the bar, and a puff of steam comes out with the boy carrying a tray. The man's eyes follow it until it shuts, then come back.

"You say the name, I knock, and he says yes or no. If it's no, you go back up and finish your drink, and you don't come round asking again." He turns the little fish over and looks at the half-cut side. "If it's yes, you go down alone. No blade out. No animal."

He tips his head a fraction toward the cat. He doesn't sound unkind about it. It's a rule, the same as the rope.

Then he puts the knife flat against the wood and keeps his eyes on James a moment longer than a doorman's usually stay on a man.

"Lot of people come asking for that name since the thaw. Most of them heard it from somebody who heard it from somebody." His voice stays low, pitched under the singing. "So how'd you get it?"

turns.message:
“Off the back of an ivory card pinned by the gate. Two-faced lady on the front, gold and dark circles on the back.”

He picks up the knife again but doesn't cut. He turns it so the lamplight runs down the blade, and looks at that instead of at James.

"One took it down, a month back. Kept it. Walked in here with it in his coat like it was a ticket." The blade turns back. "He didn't go down. Card was on the board again next morning, same tack. Nobody saw who put it up."

"So. You read it, you left it. That's the right way." He looks up properly now, and for the first time his eyes settle on the cat. It hasn't moved from its place a pace behind James's heel and it's still staring at the iron-banded door. "Midnight, then. You'll hear the bells from the quay. You come to me, I knock. He says yes or no. Not me."

He sets the point of the knife into the fish's flank and starts the next scale.

"And that one finds somewhere else to sit when you go down. Not her bar, either. She'll have its tail off."

Behind James the singers have stopped and started again. The dice hit the wall. Over the noise, from somewhere out on the quay, a single bell strikes the half before nine. Midnight is still three hours and more away.

“Midnight, then.”

The second door opens onto a room just big enough for what Marta promised. There's a bed with a straw mattress and a grey blanket that smells of lye, a three-legged stool, and a basin on a shelf with a crack mended in pitch. The ceiling slopes under the roof. Its one window is a shutter about two feet square on a leather hinge. When James opens it he sees the alley behind the kitchen, a dozen feet below. It's wet cobbles and a midden heap, and the latch-door he saw from the bar lets out onto it. A man could drop down there, but he'd land in the midden. turns.reply:
James lies back on the straw with his boots on. The blanket smells of lye and the roof timbers creak a little as they cool. Under the floor the taproom carries on: the dice, a shout, a chair scraping. The singers have given up on the second verse for good.

The cat lies against his hip, warm and heavy, with its chin on its paws and its eyes on the door.

Somewhere in the second quarter after nine, a stair creaks.

It isn't the kind of creak a drunk makes on his way up to the floor, or the boy carrying hot water. It's a single creak, and then nothing for a long moment, the way someone stops when a board gives them away. Then the next step comes, slow and careful, with the weight kept to the wall side where the treads are quieter.

The cat's head comes up off its paws. Every line of it goes stiff, and its tail wraps tight around its feet on the blanket. It doesn't make a sound. It stares at the door.

The steps reach the top of the stair. They pass the first door without slowing and stop outside the second.

A rushlight burns in a niche on the landing, and its light makes a thin yellow line under James's door. Two shadows break that line now, side by side, the width of a pair of feet. Whoever it is stands there and doesn't knock or speak. James hears a soft scuff of cloth against the wood, as if a shoulder or an ear has been laid against the planks. The iron bolt stays in its staple.

The shadows stay three breaths, maybe four.

Then they move off the line of light. The steps go back the way they came, quicker now and less careful. Whoever it is isn't hiding anymore, only leaving. They're too light for Marta and too steady for anyone who's been drinking. The stair creaks once more near the bottom, and then the taproom noise swallows them.

The cat doesn't relax. It keeps staring at the door, at the strip of rushlight under it, which is unbroken again.

Out on the quay the bells haven't rung the hour yet. Midnight is still more than two hours off.

James looks out through the cat's eyes, low against the wet stone. The latch-door is a dark slab of planking, taller than a house from down here, and the warm air leaking under it smells of eel, pepper, tallow, lye and the sweat of the boy who carries the bowls. The cat stays put and breathes it all in, sorting the smells one at a time.

The cat's head comes up off the gap at once. It goes stiff from ears to tail and stays that way. Then it puts its nose back to the bottom corner of the doorframe, to a low spot on the wood where a hand or a hip would brush going through, and sniffs it a second time, hard. Out of all the eel and pepper and lye it has found the one thread it wanted. Whoever stood outside James's door came in this way tonight, through the alley and past the kitchen.

James can't smell any of it. He can only feel the cat's certainty and see where its nose stays.

The latch rattles. The cat flattens against the wall as the door swings out a foot. The kitchen boy leans out with a bucket and slings eel-heads and grey water across the cobbles toward the midden. He's already turning back when a cat-shaped shadow slips through the gap between his heel and the frame. He never looks down. The door bangs shut on its latch.

Inside, the kitchen is hot and close, a world of table legs and the underside of a scarred board. A cook's clogs shuffle past, and a pot hisses somewhere overhead. The cat doesn't stop to look at any of it. It keeps low along the wall, under a rack of hanging pans, to the swing door into the taproom, and waits there. When the boy shoulders through with a tray, it goes through in his shadow.

The taproom from boot height is a forest of legs and lamplight through smoke. The singers are still at the first verse. The cat keeps to the dark under the end of the bar, where Marta's boots never seem to come.

It goes rigid again.

It's staring at a man at the near end of the bar, by the front door. He's young, twenty perhaps, and slight. He wears a dark wool coat over a dockhand's smock, but the smock is too clean and so are his hands. A flat cap is pulled low. He's standing, not sitting, with a small beer half gone in front of him, and every few breaths his eyes go to the foot of the narrow stair and away again. His shoes are soft-soled. They make no more noise on the boards than the cat's paws do.

He drinks off the rest of the beer in two swallows, sets a copper beside the mug and pulls the cap a little lower. Then he goes out by the red front door, not the kitchen, without a word to anyone. The cold off the quay comes in after him.

At the far end of the bar, the cellar-door man's knife has stopped in the middle of a scale. He's watching the red door swing shut. Then his eyes drop to the shadow under the bar, straight to the cat, and stay there for a long, flat moment. He doesn't say anything. He goes back to his fish.

The cat is already moving. It doesn't wait for another order, because it has one already. It slips between two drinkers' boots to the red door and waits for the next man coming in, then goes out round his ankles into the night.

The quay is dark and wet, lit by a lamp here and there and by the yellow windows behind. The young man in the cap is twenty paces ahead, maybe sixty feet. He's walking fast but not running, heading left along the water toward the ropewalk and the fish sheds, the way James came in. The cat follows along the foot of the house-fronts, from shadow to shadow, keeping the distance.

Lying on the straw upstairs, James feels the link to the cat thin out as the distance grows. It's like holding a line that is paying out through his fingers, faster than he'd like.

*(Aside: the cat's senses reach James out to 100 feet. Beyond that he loses its eyes and ears and can't send it new orders, though it will go on with the last one by its own judgement.)*

Before the link fades, I send one last instruction: *Follow him quietly. See where he goes and who he meets, but don't enter anywhere you can't easily escape. Then come back to our room.*

I release the borrowed senses and open the shutter enough for the cat to return, then wait beside it.
turns.reply:
James gives the order while the link still holds, quietly, the way he'd pass a word to a scout before the man moved out of earshot.

*Follow him. Quietly. See where he goes and who he meets. Don't go in anywhere you can't get out of easily. Then come home.*

Out on the quay the cat doesn't break stride, but its ears flick back once toward the Mermaid. James feels the order land. Then he lets go of the cat's senses before the distance takes them from him. The wet stone and the forest of boots fade, and the smell of the world goes with them. He's lying on straw under a sloping ceiling again. The bolt is in its staple and the line of rushlight under the door is unbroken.

He gets up and works the shutter open about a hand's width, then wedges it with the three-legged stool so the leather hinge can't swing it shut. Cold comes in off the alley, along with the midden smell and the steam from the kitchen door. He sits on the end of the bed beside the window and waits.

Waiting is most of scouting, and he learned that in Tethyr. Downstairs the dice hit the wall and the singers finally give up and are replaced by an argument. A cart goes along the quay with one bad wheel. Ten bells come up off the water, slow and wet. Somewhere below in the alley a door opens, and the kitchen boy throws out another bucket.

A quarter of an hour after ten bells there's a scrape on the wall outside, claws on old brick, and then nothing. A moment later the cat is in the gap of the shutter. It came up the wall the hard way, from the midden to the sill, and it pulls itself through onto the inside ledge without a sound. Its fur is beaded with damp. Its paws are black with the street. It isn't hurt, and it isn't hurrying.

It has something in its mouth.

It steps down from the ledge onto the bed and sets the thing down beside James's hand, the way a cat leaves a mouse. Then it sits back and wraps its tail around its paws.

It's a playing card.

It isn't ivory this time, just cheap pasteboard, damp along one edge from the cat's teeth. The back is printed in faded red ink with a little three-masted ship, the kind of deck any market stall in the Gate sells by the dozen. The face is the six of cups. It's an ordinary card, and James has held a thousand like it.

He's also made a thousand marks like the one on it. The top left corner has a tiny bend in it, pressed in with a thumbnail. A player who isn't looking for it never feels it. A dealer who put it there feels it every time it passes through her fingers. Somebody has been dealing with this deck who likes to know where the sixes are.

The Coin of Tymora lies warm and ordinary against his breastbone. There's nothing old about this card and no magic in it. Someone dropped it from a sharp's deck, and the cat thought it worth carrying home a long way.

The cat doesn't look at the card. It turns on the blanket and settles facing the window. It's looking at the gap in the shutter and the dark beyond it, uphill, past the alley roofs toward the city wall and the southern gate.

Downstairs, someone wins at dice and roars. Midnight is still more than an hour and a half off.

I crouch beside the cat and hold out a hand for it to sniff.

*Good work. Did he meet the woman dealing cards at the gate?* I picture her face as I ask through our bond. *Can you show me—or help me understand—where he stopped?*

turns.reply:
James crouches by the bed and holds out his hand, knuckles down. The cat leans in and sniffs it, the way it would check any hand that's been somewhere new. Then it pushes the top of its damp head hard against his knuckles, once, and pulls back. It's as close to praise returned as he's going to get.

He thinks the question at it and holds the dealer's face in his mind the way he saw it at the gate: the quick smile, the hands that never stopped moving, the eyes that went to his purse before they went to his face.

No words come back along the bond. They never do. The cat goes still the moment the face takes shape in his head. Its ears come forward and its tail wraps tight around its paws.

Then it reaches out one forepaw and sets it on the six of cups, square in the middle of the card, and presses down until the pasteboard lies flat on the blanket. It keeps the paw there and looks him in the eye.

It holds that for a breath. Then it takes its paw back, steps over the card without touching it again and jumps to the window ledge. It pushes its head into the gap he wedged open in the shutter, and the cold from the alley comes in around it. It isn't looking down at the midden or along the alley. It's looking up and to the left, over the wet roofs of the alley houses, toward where the street climbs back to the wall. It's looking at the dark place above the chimney smoke where the southern gatehouse stands, though nothing of it can be seen from this window.

It looks back over its shoulder at James, then turns uphill again and keeps looking.

It doesn't jump down, and it doesn't come back to the bed. It stays on the sill with its tail around its paws and the night air ruffling the damp fur on its back. It's the stillness he's learned to read on the road. It means *there*, and the cat is waiting to see what he'll do about it.

Under the floor the dice hit the wall. Out on the water no bell has rung since the quarter. Midnight is still an hour and three quarters off.

I tuck the card into an outer pocket, away from my own deck, and let the cat back inside before closing the shutter. I stay in the bolted room until a few minutes before midnight, then head down to the doorman, leaving the cat resting on the bed.

turns.reply:
"So she had someone follow us." James looks down at the six of cups on the grey blanket. "We'll leave her waiting for a change."

He picks it up by the edges and slips it into the outer pocket of his coat, on the opposite side from his own deck. The two shouldn't touch.

At the window the cat pulls its head back in from the gap. For a moment it stays on the ledge, still looking uphill, before it steps down onto the bed. James takes the stool out of the shutter and the leather hinge swings the shutter closed on the alley. The midden smell stays in the room a while longer than the cold does.

After that he just waits.

The waiting is long. The straw rustles whenever he shifts his weight. The rushlight on the landing burns down and somebody replaces it, because the line under the door goes dark, then comes back brighter and steadier. Nobody stops outside. Under the floor the argument that replaced the singers has burned itself out, and the room has settled into the low steady mutter of a tavern that won't close so much as run out of customers. The dice ring breaks up some time after ten. Eleven bells come up off the water, and later the half after eleven. Somebody goes up the stair heavily, laughing at nothing, and bangs the first door shut. It's a drunk, nothing like the earlier footsteps, and the cat barely lifts its head.

Shortly after the quarter before midnight James gets up off the bed. He checks that the rapier sits right in its scabbard, buttons the purse inside his coat and draws the bolt as quietly as iron allows.

The cat has stood up on the blanket. It's facing him, not the door.

*Wait here. I'll come back for you.*

It holds his eye for a breath. Then it lies down again in the hollow his body left in the straw, wraps its tail tight around its paws and turns to face the door. It stays that way while he steps out and pulls the door shut behind him. The key turns in the lock from outside.

The taproom has thinned to perhaps a dozen people. The singers are gone. The fourth man was carried out or woke and walked out, and their booth is a wreck of mugs. Two sailors are asleep upright by the cold end of the hearth. Somebody is playing a slow game of knucklebones alone, a few old men are finishing their last cups, and a dockhand stands at the bar with his head in his hands. Marta is wiping down the far end of the bar and doesn't look up as he passes. Garrow's table by the hearth is empty.

At the dim end of the room the broad man is still on his stool beside the iron-banded door. The little fish in his hand has more scales now, and the pile of shavings on his knee has grown. He finishes the scale he's on. Then he looks up at James, past him toward the stair, and down at the empty floor by James's heel.

He gives a small nod, as if James has got the first part right.

Midnight comes up off the quay one stroke at a time, slow and wet, the sound carrying in under the red door. The doorman waits for the last of the twelve strokes. Then he sets the knife and the fish down on the stool, stands, and knocks on the black door with the side of his fist: two knocks, a pause, one more.

For a while nothing happens. James can hear the sleeping sailors breathing, and the knucklebones clicking on the table behind him.

Then there's a voice from beyond the door, below it and a long way down, as if it has come up a stair. It's a man's voice, dry and unhurried.

"Who's asking?"

"Card reader." The doorman keeps his own voice low and never takes his eyes off James. "Read it at the gate. Put it back after. Came in tonight, sat with the hook-man, came to me first and asked how it's done."

The silence below goes on longer this time.

"The one with the cat?"

The doorman's eyes flick to the empty floor again. "Left it upstairs."

Somewhere below, something small is set down on wood.

"Yes," the voice says. "Send him down."

The doorman takes a key from inside his smock, iron and as long as a hand, and fits it into the big keyhole. The lock turns with a sound like a heavy drawer closing. He pulls the door open toward himself. Cold air comes out, smelling of tarred hemp, wet stone and lamp oil. Beyond the door a narrow stair goes down between brick walls, each step worn hollow in the middle. A single lamp burns at the bottom, below the curve of the wall where James can't see.

The doorman stands aside with the door in his hand.

"Blade stays sheathed. Hands where he can see them." He looks James over one last time, quickly, the way he looked at him at nine. "I'm up here the whole time."

He holds the door and waits.

note.text:
The atmosphere worked very well. The gate queue, Garrow’s muddy coat, Marta’s room key, the doorman carving his fish—all gave me people and places I could picture and respond to. Refusing the card game felt like a meaningful character choice without making James’s weakness take over the opening. Taking down the ivory card, reading it, and putting it back also felt like a choice the world noticed.

Garrow was the strongest scene for me. His concern gave James a reason to care beyond “my goddess sent me,” and the missing ring and false Fist attendant were concrete clues worth investigating. I also appreciated having time to eat, secure a room, learn the entrances, and approach the midnight meeting on my own terms.

What broke or dragged:
- **The opening was very slow.** We spent the whole session reaching the door of the first substantial meeting. I’d have preferred to meet Hollis and hear the initial proposition before the cutoff.
- **Raw tool-call markup appeared in the narration**, including a supposedly private watcher roll. That exposed information James didn’t know and interrupted the scene.
- **Some rules and numbers were inconsistent.** Perception was rolled at +2 despite the sheet’s +1; Healing Light was capped at four dice rather than the campaign sheet’s five. A quick reconciliation at the start would help.
- The repeated descriptions—tails wrapped tightly, slow wet bells, dice hitting the wall, people testing words “like a rope”—became noticeable. They were evocative initially, but repetition stretched scenes.

What I missed was an early sense of the campaign’s promised crew-and-heist direction. The mysteries are interesting, but I’m still waiting to learn what James might actually be asked to do. A concrete offer would give me something to plan around.

Overall, I wanted to keep playing. Keep the grounded NPCs, consequences, and investigable clues; compress uneventful waiting and repeated atmosphere, and let the first session deliver a clear proposition alongside the mystery.

after.text:
Yes—when the cat came back with the marked six and pointed toward the gate, I wanted to go find Tamsin and confront her about having James followed.

I stayed because midnight had been established as the important appointment, and I didn’t know whether a trip uphill would make me miss it. I also wanted to reach Hollis before the session ended. That was partly James being cautious, partly me protecting our progress toward the main hook.

The temptation worked: I was genuinely curious about Tamsin. What held me back was pacing and uncertainty about travel time, rather than a lack of interest.

The sun is sliding down behind the Outer City and the shadows of the gatehouse stretch across the Trade Way. The queue shuffles forward a cart's length at a time: a family with their whole life on a handcart, a dwarf swearing at his mule, two sellswords comparing scars. Up ahead, under the arch, a Flaming Fist sergeant with a ledger and a tired voice asks everyone the same thing: name, business, how long you're staying.

From the side of the road comes a familiar sound — cards being shuffled. A lean young woman has turned a crate into a table and is dealing for anyone with copper to lose. "Short wait, quick game, friend! Lady Luck's smiling tonight!" Her eyes have already found James's coat and the weight of his purse.

At your feet the cat has gone very still. It is not looking at the cards on the crate. It is looking at the notice board beside the gate, where, between a wanted poster and a notice about curfew in the Upper City, someone has pinned a single playing card — face out, alone, without a word of explanation.

The sergeant looks up from his ledger. "Next." Two more travellers and it will be you.
